problem: Advanced topology-based VLN agents (e.g. DUET) may not really exploit visual content: as in VQA/EQA, gains from richer visual representations may not come from better grounding, and how visual quality versus model capacity (branches) drives generalization is unclear.
motivation: Prior work shows vision is underused in vision-language tasks (language priors, insensitivity to visual change). If VLN agents are similarly insensitive, then improving generalization needs a controlled study of visual perturbations and branch expansion. The authors observe that replacing inputs with perturbed or noisy views barely hurts and that adding branches helps.
key_idea: Extend a dual-branch topology-based VLN agent (DUET) into a multi-branch architecture in which ancillary branches receive perturbed, depth or noise visual inputs and are fused with learnable weights, showing that branch expansion plus perturbed views improves generalization.
insight: The heatmap ablations show both factors matter: adding branches with even random noise raises REVERIE val-unseen SPL from 35.75 to 36.92, and perturbed-view ancillary branches reach 39.80. Table ablation: MBA alone gives 37.66 and MBA+perturbed views 39.80 (CLIP encoder), so the two are synergistic. More branches with original RGB are not always better (37.66 vs 38.09 for a single extra branch), suggesting noise acts as a regularizer against over-reliance on RGB; the mechanism is not established.
method: Visual perturbation strategies: four inputs per view: original CLIP-ViT-L/14@336px RGB features (OG), ground-truth depth features from ResNet-152 projected to 768-d by an FFN (D), perturbed view v_PV=(1-γ)v_OG+γ v_IV mixing an incongruent view (γ=0.5), and random noise vector in R^768 (RN).

Base dual-branch agent: DUET local branch (LXMERT-style cross-modal encoding of current panorama, predicting adjacent ghost nodes) and global branch (topological map encoding, allowing backtracking) fused by dynamic fusion.

Multi-branch architecture (MBA): adds ancillary local/global branches that share the single-branch structure but take different visual inputs; the best setting uses perturbed-view inputs for the ancillary branches (four branches in total).

Multi-branch aggregation: learnable weights λ from Softmax(Sigmoid(FFN)) over the 0-th hidden token of each branch; per-branch scores from a two-layer FFN; P_l and P_g are weighted sums, then DynamicFuse(P_l, P_g).

Training: pre-training with MLM, MRC and SAP as in DUET/LAD; fine-tuning loss = μ CE(P_a, a_gt) + CE(P_a, a*) + CE(P_o, o_gt) with DAgger-style pseudo-target a* and μ=0.2; perturbations applied only during training analysis of visual inputs, not to instructions or object features; 25k iterations on one RTX 4090.

numbers_note: R2R main table prints SR/SPL as integers. Ablation and heatmap numbers (e.g. 36.92, 38.82) are in figures or text only and are not listed as separate rows.
results: MBA on DUET reaches REVERIE val-unseen SPL 39.80 (vs DUET* 33.73 and CLIP-DUET 35.75) and test-unseen SPL 39.53, beating VER (39.66 val-unseen SPL). On SOON it outperforms GOAT (val-unseen SPL 29.57 vs 28.05). R2R gains are marginal (val-unseen SR 73, SPL 63).
limitations: The mechanism behind gains from noisy/perturbed branches is not explained; the regularization explanation is speculative.
Optimal perturbation was chosen on REVERIE and applied to R2R/SOON even though it may not be optimal there; R2R gains are small.
Added branches increase parameters and compute; only topology-based agents (DUET, DSRG, LAD) were tested.
